tour.title: West Street, Karst Peaks & a Ride to the Yulong
tour.summary: A town walk that turns into a country ride: a sixth-century street, a locals' park, a painter's house and the Li River on foot, then a rented bicycle south through the karst to the Ten-Mile Gallery, Moon Hill and the old Yulong valley village.
tour.overviewText:
Yangshuo exists because of the rock. The town sits on the Li River in Guangxi, the Zhuang Autonomous Region of southern China, inside a forest of limestone towers that rise straight out of the fields. Geologists call the style tower karst; the Chinese call it fenglin, "peak forest". The rock began as seabed roughly 320 to 400 million years ago — thousands of metres of it, unusually pure — was lifted by tectonic pressure, and then dissolved slowly by rainwater turned faintly acidic. What is left is the skeleton: hundreds of peaks, thousands of caves, and a river threading between them. In 2014 UNESCO inscribed the landscape as part of the South China Karst World Heritage Site.

For most of its history Yangshuo was a market town and river port. It has been a county seat since 590 CE, when a street was laid out here that is now West Street. In the 1980s it became one of the first places in China where independent foreign travellers could stop, and a generation of backpackers and English teachers gave it English menus and the nickname "Global Village". That foreign scene has since thinned; the crowds are now overwhelmingly domestic, and the county reported more than twenty-one million visitor arrivals in 2023. Guangxi is officially a Zhuang region — the Zhuang are China's largest ethnic minority, a Tai-speaking people — but the everyday speech here is a local Southwestern Mandarin, and the money in your pocket is the yuan (¥), also called RMB.

This tour has two halves, and they move differently. The first is a walk: about four kilometres through the town, from West Street to Yangshuo Park, the painter Xu Beihong's former house, the Li River waterfront, the carved cliff of Bilian Peak and the riverside stage where Impression Liu Sanjie is performed. The second half is a bicycle ride: you rent a bike in town and pedal south out of the karst basin to Gongnong Bridge and the Ten-Mile Gallery, detour to the arched peak of Moon Hill, then follow the Yulong River valley north-west to the rice paddies at Jima and the old village of Jiuxian. End to end the route runs about twenty-five kilometres.

This is why you need a bike. The country legs alone are about twenty kilometres, and on foot the same route would take more than seven hours, much of it on the shoulder of the 321 highway — so do not try to walk it. Rent a bicycle in Yangshuo: shops on West Street and Guihua Road rent simple city bikes for roughly ¥20–50 a day and better mountain bikes for ¥50–70, and you should check the brakes and gears before you set out. Carry water and small yuan notes, set up WeChat Pay or Alipay, and start the ride by late morning. Every fee, hour and price below is a guide, not a promise.

You are walking and riding through a landscape that took three hundred million years to make and about thirty to turn into an attraction. Go slowly, look up, and get out of town.
tour.difficulty: Easy on foot, moderate by bike. The town half is flat stone-slab lanes plus two short stepped climbs — the Woyun Pavilion in Yangshuo Park and the summit of Bilian Peak. The country half is a bicycle ride of about twenty kilometres on flat but rough lanes and the shoulder of the 321 road, with traffic, plus the short climb to Moon Hill's arch. Do not attempt the countryside on foot: the same legs would take more than seven hours.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start on West Street around 08:00–09:00, before the crush, and do the town on foot before the heat builds. Then rent a bike by late morning and ride south to the Ten-Mile Gallery and up the Yulong valley, reaching Jiuxian for the afternoon light on the paddies, and ride back to town before dark — the country lanes are unlit and the buffalo have right of way. Impression Liu Sanjie plays back in town at about 20:00, so see it on whichever evening suits. In June, build the day around the rain — mornings are often the clearest hours.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: West Street
stops.narration:
Look down first. The stone under your feet is the oldest thing on this street that still does its original job: big slabs, worn shiny in the middle where a great many feet have passed. Yangshuo became a county in 590 CE, under the Sui dynasty, and the record says a street was laid out here then — five metres wide, two hundred long. That street is the one you are standing on. West Street, Xi Jie in Chinese, is the spine of the old town, running east from here to the Li River.

What stands above the slabs is younger. Most of these buildings are sixty or seventy years old, with a few survivors from the Ming and Qing dynasties mixed in — timber upper floors, tiled roofs, balconies leaning over the lane. Look above the shop signs: that is where the real street is, not in the souvenir racks.

Because the story of West Street is what happened to it in the last forty years. In the 1980s, as China began opening to independent travellers, Yangshuo became one of the first places a foreigner with a backpack could get off a bus, and the town discovered it liked them. By the 1990s most of the shops on this street were run by foreigners, and locals — unusually for a Chinese town this size — learned enough English to deal with them. The street picked up the nickname Yangren Jie, Foreigners' Street, and later Diqiu Cun, Global Village. Climbing came next: the limestone around town turned out to be world-class, and Yangshuo acquired another title, the climbing capital of China, with more than three hundred bolted routes on the crags outside town.

Now walk it as it is today. The county reported over twenty-one million visitor arrivals in 2023, and the crowd is overwhelmingly Chinese now, not foreign. The English menus survive, the beer fish survives — the local signature dish, a whole river fish braised with beer, chilli and tomato — and so does the tension: this is a working county town of about three hundred thousand people whose economy now depends on visitors enjoying its old street. Buy something, pay a fair price, and you are part of the arrangement rather than just photographing it.

Hours are almost meaningless here because the street never closes; shops run roughly nine in the morning to eleven at night. Come back after dark, when it is lantern-lit and loud, or come at seven in the morning when it belongs to delivery carts and grandmothers. Then walk west, away from the river, toward the green hills and the town park.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Shops, bars and restaurants charge normal prices; bargaining is fine in the souvenir stalls.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours. Shops run roughly 09:00 to 23:00; the street is busiest from mid-afternoon into the night.
stops.accessibility: Level pedestrian lane of large stone slabs — uneven in places, no vehicles, and very crowded in the evening. Wheelchairs manage the middle but will bump on raised slabs.
stops.insiderTip: Look above the shop signs at the timber upper floors and tiled roofs — most are sixty or seventy years old, a few are genuine Ming and Qing work. Then come back at 07:00, when the street belongs to delivery carts.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west along West Street, away from the river, for about seven hundred metres; the lane runs on into Diecui Road and the green hills close in. The gate of Yangshuo Park opens on your left with the peaks rising behind it. That is our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Imcall, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Yangshuo Park
stops.narration:
Step off the tourist street and into the town's living room. Yangshuo Park is where locals come to do tai chi at dawn, play cards under the trees all afternoon and walk the paths in the evening; it is the same twenty-two hectares of garden the town has kept since 1915, when it was laid out and named Shouyang Park after Shouyang Mountain, the old name of the peak by the river. It was renamed Yangshuo Park in 1934, and the characters over the gate were brushed by the painter Liu Haisu in 1978.

The park is built around three small limestone hills — Xilang Mountain, Duxiu Peak and Zhongling Mountain — and a stream, the Double Moon, that wanders through the middle. Each hill carries a pavilion: the Huixian, the Fanghe, and the Woyun, the "Resting Cloud" Pavilion, which is where you are heading. There are caves in the rock too — the Dragon Cave, the Bilian Cave, the Laixian Cave — and the Ming-dynasty travel writer Xu Xiake, who came through Guangxi in 1637 and is the closest thing China has to a founding father of geology, poked around them and wrote them up. Three and a half centuries before UNESCO noticed, a Chinese scholar was already taking the karst seriously.

Now climb. The path up to the Woyun Pavilion is short, maybe ten minutes of steps, and it is not the famous viewpoint — almost no visitor comes here — but it does something the famous viewpoints cannot. From the top you look down on the whole town at once: the grey roofs and white walls packed between the hills, West Street a thread, the Li River bending past the eastern edge, and the karst towers standing in the haze in every direction. This is the geography of Yangshuo in one look: a small town that fits entirely inside a valley of limestone peaks, because flat land here is scarce and every building has to squeeze onto it.

Study the towers while you have the height. Each one is the leftover of a limestone plateau that has been dissolving for millions of years, and the flat ground you are standing above is what was carried away. The Chinese name for the landscape, fenglin, means "peak forest", but from up here the more useful word is archipelago: islands of rock in a sea of flat farmland, which is close to how the first European geologists described it.

The park is free, open from early morning until well after dark, and genuinely used — which is the point. Sit for ten minutes and watch. In a town that now lives on visitors, this is one of the few places where the visitors are the minority. Then come down, cross Diecui Road, and head back into the lanes to a small house where a famous painter once lived.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry, open from early morning until well after dark.
stops.openingHours: Open daily from early morning until well after dark. Liveliest at dawn, when locals do tai chi, and in the cool of the evening.
stops.accessibility: Paved paths and steps. The main paths are level, but the climb to the Woyun Pavilion is a short flight of uneven stone steps — not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Climb to the Woyun Pavilion for the town panorama — almost no visitors bother, and it is the only place you see all of Yangshuo at once. Dawn is when the park belongs to the locals.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come down from the pavilion, leave the park by the main gate and turn back east into the lanes — about eight hundred metres, past the market end of the old town, toward the county government quarter. Xu Beihong's house is on Xianqian Street, a low grey building with a plaque over the door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Immanuel Giel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Xu Beihong Residence
stops.narration:
Here is a small house with a large claim on modern Chinese art. Xu Beihong lived in this courtyard in 1936 and 1937, and while he was here he styled himself a commoner of Yangshuo. The house is modest — a single-storey, three-bay brick-and-timber building around a courtyard with a white magnolia tree, a parlour, a studio and a bedroom — and it was restored in 1984, when the plaque over the door was written by his widow, Liao Jingwen.

Know who he was. Xu Beihong, born in Yixing in Jiangsu in 1895 and dead in Beijing in 1953, is the painter every Chinese schoolchild can name, mostly for his ink paintings of galloping horses. But the horses are the least interesting thing about him. He spent years studying in Paris at the École des Beaux-Arts, where he was known as Ju Péon, and came home convinced that Chinese painting had grown too inward — too much copying of old masters, too little looking at the world. His answer was to fuse the two traditions: Chinese brush and ink, Western anatomy, perspective and light. He painted horses because he could make them move, and he painted people at monumental scale because he believed art should carry history.

That argument is why this house matters. In the 1930s Chinese art was split between traditionalists, who wanted to defend the literati brush, and reformers like Xu, who wanted realism and Western training. Xu won in the institutions: he became the first president of the Central Academy of Fine Arts and is counted one of the "Four Great Academy Presidents" who built modern Chinese art education. Almost every serious Chinese painter since has been taught in a system he shaped.

And here, specifically, he painted the karst. While he was in Yangshuo he made "Spring Rain on the Li River" and other landscapes of these towers and this water — the landscape you have been walking through, looked at by an eye trained in Paris. Stand in the courtyard and hold that thought: a place can be painted for a thousand years and still be seen anew, because the person looking changes.

Entry is free and the house is small — give it twenty minutes, more if a caretaker is chatty. Hours are modest and can shift, so check at the door. Then step through the lanes to the riverbank, which is only a block away, and turn south to follow the water.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry. Hours are modest and can shift; verify at the door.
stops.openingHours: Small memorial hours, roughly daytime, and often closed one day a week. Check before counting on it.
stops.accessibility: A single-storey house around a level courtyard, with a step at the door and uneven old paving. The rooms are small.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the white magnolia in the courtyard and the plaque written by his widow, Liao Jingwen. Ask the caretaker about "Spring Rain on the Li River" — the landscape he painted from here.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the house and walk east through the lanes to the riverbank, about a hundred metres — you will come out on Binjiang Road with the water in front of you. That stretch of promenade by the dock is the Li River waterfront, our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: ArishG, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Li River Waterfront
stops.narration:
This is the river that made the landscape and the town. The Li — Li Jiang in Chinese — rises in the Mao'er Mountains to the north, runs 164 kilometres through Guilin and Yangshuo, and then joins the Gui River and the Pearl River system on its way to the South China Sea. The stretch from Guilin down to here is about eighty-three kilometres, dropping from 141 metres above sea level at Guilin to 103 metres at Yangshuo — a lazy gradient, which is why the water runs clear over pebbles and why the classic cruise takes four hours to drift it.

Two thousand years ago this was infrastructure, not scenery. In 214 BCE, engineers of the Qin dynasty cut the Lingqu Canal to link the Li's upper reaches with the Xiang River, which flows north to the Yangtze. That joined two of China's great river systems, so grain and soldiers could move by water from the Yangtze valley all the way to the Pearl River delta. The karst was an obstacle then, a wall of limestone the canal had to thread; beauty is a much later idea.

The cruise is the set piece now. Boats leave Guilin's piers in the morning — three-star boats from Mopanshan, four-star from Zhujiang — and motor down past the named rocks: Nine Horse Painting Hill, where you are invited to find nine horses in the cliff, and Huangbu Shoal, whose reflection is printed on the back of the twenty-yuan note. Tickets run roughly ¥215 to ¥360 depending on boat class and whether meals and transfers are included; verify before you book, because packages vary wildly and the cheapest ticket often includes nothing.

You will also see, at dusk, the photograph everyone wants: a fisherman on a bamboo raft with two cormorants. Understand what you are watching. Cormorant fishing is real and old — for over a thousand years Chinese fishermen trained great cormorants, tying a loose snare around the base of the bird's throat so it can swallow small fish but not large ones, then taking the catch from its gullet. Here it survives almost entirely as a staged performance for cameras, paid by the shot. There is nothing wrong with that, but the birds are no longer working for a living and the fishermen are no longer fishing. Ask before you photograph, and pay.

The river is also the town's swimming pool. Locals swim from the steps below you, and on a hot June evening the water is the best thing in Yangshuo. Watch for the current and for the tour boats, which pass in a rooster-tail of wake.

Then turn south and walk the bank — the promenade follows the water out of town, past the old wharves, toward the peak that leans over the river ahead.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free waterfront. The Guilin–Yangshuo cruise is a separate booking, roughly ¥215–360; cormorant photo sessions are paid by the shot and should be agreed first.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours. Liveliest at dusk; locals swim in the late afternoon.
stops.accessibility: Paved riverside promenade, mostly level, with steps down to the water in places. Benches along the bank.
stops.insiderTip: Dusk is the cormorant hour — the staged photos happen on the bank and on rafts. Agree the price before you raise a camera. If you swim, watch for the wake of the Guilin tour boats, which pass mainly in the early afternoon.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south along Binjiang Road for about three hundred metres, following the river with the water on your left. The garden gate at the foot of the peak ahead — the Yangshuo Cultural Relics Landscape Garden — is Bilian Peak, our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Luka Peternel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Bilian Peak
stops.narration:
You are at the foot of Yangshuo's own mountain. This is Bilian Peak — Green Lotus Peak — the hill that dominates the town, named for the way it looks from the river: a lotus bud about to open, and when the water is still, a second lotus opening upside down in the reflection. For centuries that reflection has been one of the eight classic views of Yangshuo.

The peak is limestone, like everything around it, and it has been a place of inscriptions for at least five hundred years. Its older name was Jianshan, and it was renamed in the Ming dynasty, in the Jiajing period, when a provincial official named Hong Zhu carved the characters for Bilian Peak into the rock. Since then the cliff has collected more carving than any other in town, and the strangest is the one to hunt for: a single character, dai — "belt" — written in one flowing stroke of cursive calligraphy by Wang Yuanren, a magistrate from Zhejiang, in 1834, and cut into the stone by his successor. It is nearly six metres tall and covers some seventeen square metres, and nobody is quite sure what it means. The popular reading is that one character is meant to hold a whole phrase, "a belt of rivers and mountains", the landscape itself, but that is interpretation, not inscription.

At the foot of the peak, just west of the garden gate, stands a small hall built in 1931 to remember a single day. On 29 November 1921 Sun Yat-sen — the revolutionary who founded the Republic of China — came up the Li River to Yangshuo on his way to Guilin, spent the night at the county's higher primary school, and spoke to the assembled townspeople from a classroom corridor. He called his talk "Implement the Three Principles of the People and Develop Yangshuo's Resources", and in it he told the town that it was rich: "Yangshuo is golden everywhere." He meant the landscape and what it could earn — a striking thing to read on a wall in a town that now lives almost entirely on the scenery he praised. Within four years he was dead, and the country fell into decades more of division and war; the hall is a county's memory of the day the founder of the republic came to town.

To see the carvings you enter the small riverside garden at the base of the peak, the Yangshuo Cultural Relics Landscape Garden, converted from an old riverside park and stacked with more than twenty historical steles, including the line every Chinese schoolchild knows — "Guilin's scenery is the best under heaven". The gate price is quoted around ¥30 for adults, with student and senior rates, and it is usually open roughly 08:30 to 17:30; prices and hours move, so check at the window. The Ming travel writer Xu Xiake came through here in the seventeenth century and called the view "a world of jade lotus and bamboo shoots".

Then climb. A path on the north-west flank leads up through the trees to the summit, about 298 metres above sea level — call it two hundred metres of steps, twenty or thirty minutes up, and slippery when wet. From the top the whole town lies below you: the Li River bending around the peak, West Street a grey thread, and karst towers standing in the haze in every direction, each one the leftover of a limestone plateau that has been dissolving for millions of years. This is the best single view in town, and almost nobody climbs it. Bring water, take the steps slowly, and remember that wet limestone is a skating rink.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Garden gate price quoted around ¥30 for adults, with student and senior rates; some ticket channels sell it for less. Prices and hours move — verify at the window.
stops.openingHours: Typically 08:30 to 17:30 daily; the summit path is inside the ticketed garden. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible, honestly: the summit path is steep, uneven stone steps, slippery when wet. The riverside garden and its carved steles are on level ground.
stops.insiderTip: Hunt the giant cursive dai character on the cliff — one stroke, nearly six metres tall, carved in 1834 and debated ever since. Then climb: almost nobody does, and it is the best view in town.
stops.nextStopDirections: Back at the gate, turn south and follow the riverbank out of town — about two kilometres, past the old wharves and across the Yangshuo Bridge, to the open-air stage on the far bank. That is the Impression Liu Sanjie theatre, the last stop in town. It is flat the whole way but has traffic; a taxi is cheap if you would rather ride.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: BMSBridge, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Impression Liu Sanjie Theatre
stops.narration:
You have walked out to the edge of town for China's first real-scenery performance. Impression Liu Sanjie — Yinxiang Liu Sanjie in Chinese — is staged here on the Li River, and the set is not a set: a dozen karst peaks stand behind the water, lit as the backdrop, and the river itself is the stage. It was directed by Zhang Yimou, the film-maker behind Hero and the 2008 Beijing Olympics opening ceremony, together with Wang Chaoge and Fan Yue, and it opened in 2004. It is the show that invented a genre — dozens of "Impression" productions in other Chinese cities followed it.

Who is Liu Sanjie? She is a legendary singer of the Zhuang people, the Tai-speaking ethnic group who give Guangxi its name: a folk heroine, called the "song fairy", said to have lived in the Tang dynasty and to have answered every challenge with a song. A famous 1960 film made her a household name across China, and this show turns her story into music and movement on the water, with a cast of more than six hundred performers, many of them farmers and fisherfolk from the villages around Yangshuo, working in Zhuang, Miao and Yao dress.

Watch how the staging uses what is already there. There is no proscenium and no roof; boats cross the water as the singers work, and the peaks that have been the backdrop to your whole day become the scenery of the performance. It runs about seventy minutes and usually starts around eight in the evening. Face-value tickets are around ¥188, often discounted through hotels and booking apps, and there are premium seats and cheaper ones; verify prices and times when you book, because they move with the season.

The show plays at night, which is why this is the last stop of the town half. You are here in daylight, so you have two choices: come back in the evening — book ahead in high season and arrive by about seven-thirty — or treat the site as what it is, the place where a county of farmers turned its own landscape into a nightly performance and made a living from it. Either way, the town is now behind you and the countryside is ahead: from here you get on a bicycle and ride south.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Face-value tickets around ¥188, often discounted; premium seats cost more. Book ahead in high season and verify prices and show times when you book.
stops.openingHours: Performances typically nightly, starting around 20:00 and running about seventy minutes; the site itself is outdoors and best viewed in the evening. Times vary by season.
stops.accessibility: The theatre is an outdoor riverside site with tiered seating and some steps; check when booking if you need step-free access.
stops.insiderTip: Arrive by about 19:30 to watch the crowd and the light, and book through a hotel or app rather than the gate for a better price. The cheap seats still see the whole river stage.
stops.nextStopDirections: The town walk ends here and the bicycle ride begins. Rent a bike in town — shops on West Street and Guihua Road rent simple city bikes for roughly ¥20–50 a day — and ride south out of Yangshuo, following the 321 road for about six kilometres to the bridge where the Yulong River meets the Li. That is Gongnong Bridge, the start of the countryside, our next stop. It is about twenty-five minutes by bike; on foot the same leg is well over an hour along a busy highway, so ride it.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gerd Eichmann, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ten-Mile Gallery & Gongnong Bridge
stops.narration:
You rode here, and that is the point of this half of the tour: from now on the countryside is a bicycle ride, not a walk. This is Gongnong Bridge, where the Yulong River — the small, shallow tributary you will follow this afternoon — empties into the Li, and where the Ten-Mile Gallery begins. It is worth pausing to understand what you are looking at, because the rocks around you are the point of the whole region.

Here is the mechanism. Around 320 to 400 million years ago this whole region was a shallow tropical sea, and it laid down thousands of metres of limestone — the compressed skeletons of corals and shellfish. Guilin's limestone is unusually pure, with porosity under one percent, which makes it strong and slow to crumble. Then tectonic uplift, driven ultimately by the collision of India with Asia, raised the seabed into a plateau, and the rain went to work. Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide from the air and the soil and becomes a weak carbonic acid, and that acid dissolves limestone along its cracks. Millions of years of that ate the plateau down into what you see: isolated towers with near-vertical sides standing on a flat plain, a style geologists call tower karst and the Chinese call fenglin, "peak forest".

There is a second style, fengcong, "peak cluster", where the peaks still share a common base with deep hollows between them; that is what you saw on the Li River upstream. Tower karst is what happens when fengcong is uplifted further and eroded longer, until the base dissolves away and the peaks become islands. Here in the Yangshuo basin the towers run 30 to 80 metres high; closer to the fengcong country they reach 300. The whole process is young in geological terms, ten to twenty million years. In 2014 this landscape was inscribed by UNESCO as part of the South China Karst World Heritage Site.

South of here the road runs through the Ten-Mile Gallery, Shili Hualang in Chinese, the stretch of scenery that made this area famous, and the limestone towers crowd in on both sides. This is also where Chinese sport climbing took hold: the cliffs here were bolted by climbers in the 1990s, and they still carry some of the hardest lines in the country. If you see climbers hanging off the rock, that is the "climbing capital" claim being tested in public.

Now get back on the bike. Follow the gallery road south-west toward the peak with the hole through it — Moon Hill, about two kilometres away. Keep the river on your right.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to ride or walk the road. Attractions along it charge separately — Moon Hill takes a small ticket; verify on the day.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all hours. The attractions along the gallery keep daytime hours.
stops.accessibility: Paved road with traffic; ride with care. The country lanes of the Yulong valley beyond are flat but uneven.
stops.insiderTip: The Yulong's mouth is right here under the bridge — look upstream where the clear tributary meets the busy Li. Then take the back lanes along the south bank, not the highway.
stops.nextStopDirections: Get back on the bike and follow the Ten-Mile Gallery road south-west for about two kilometres to the peak with the hole through it — Moon Hill, our next stop. That is ten minutes of easy pedalling; on foot the same leg is about three-quarters of an hour, so ride it.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Liuxingy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Moon Hill
stops.narration:
Here is the most photographed arch in Guangxi. Moon Hill — Yueliang Shan in Chinese — is a limestone peak with a perfect semicircular hole punched through its upper half, and the hole is a fossil: it began as a cave inside the hill, and when the cave roof collapsed, what was left was this arch, a window through the rock with sky on both sides. The Chinese call such a peak a "moon" because the opening frames the sky like a crescent, and from different points on the road below the "moon" seems to wax and wane — full from one angle, a thin crescent from another.

You are on a bicycle leg, and Moon Hill is a short climb off the route rather than a long walk: park the bike, pay the small entry fee (quoted around ¥15, and the site has closed for restoration spells, so check before you commit), and take the steep, uneven stone steps up to the arch in about twenty minutes. The view from the top is the reward: the Ten-Mile Gallery road unrolling below, the Yulong valley beyond, and the tower karst standing in every direction.

Moon Hill is also a climbing landmark. In the 1990s the American climber Todd Skinner bolted routes on these cliffs, and the lines through and around the arch became some of the hardest in China. If climbers are on the rock, watch for a minute — you are looking at the sport that gave Yangshuo its other reputation.

Then get back on the bike and turn north-west: the next stretch is the prettiest of the ride, the lanes climbing gently into the Yulong valley, with the river on your left and the paddies opening up.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Entry quoted around ¥15; the site has closed for restoration spells in recent years, so verify it is open before you count on the climb.
stops.openingHours: Daytime hours, typically roughly 08:00 to 17:30; subject to temporary closures for restoration. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible: a steep, uneven flight of stone steps to the arch. The road below and the car park are level.
stops.insiderTip: Walk a hundred metres up or down the road before you climb — the 'moon' changes shape with the angle, and the classic full-moon view is not from the ticket gate.
stops.nextStopDirections: Back on the bike, turn north-west and follow the country lanes into the Yulong valley — about seven and a half kilometres to the paddies at Jima, our next stop. That is half an hour or so of easy pedalling; on foot the same leg is well over two hours, so ride it.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: chensiyuan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Yulong Valley Paddies at Jima
stops.narration:
You are in the fields now, and this is the part of the ride worth the pedalling. The Yulong valley is the most fertile land in the county: flat, low-lying, irrigated by a river that runs clear because there is no industry upstream and, unusually, almost no motorboats — the Yulong is raft-only by local rule, which is why it is so quiet.

Start with the rice. A flooded field like these is a paddy — the word comes from padi, Malay for the rice plant — and paddy farming is a wetland technology invented in the Yangtze basin thousands of years ago and carried across Asia. In this part of Guangxi the calendar runs two crops a year. Early rice is planted around March and cut in July, in the frantic few weeks farmers call shuangqiang, the double rush, when the harvest and the replanting happen at once; the late crop goes in immediately after and is harvested in late October or November. If you are here in early summer, the fields are at their greenest — standing water and young rice — and the valley is loud with frogs at dusk.

The other field workers are water buffalo: the swamp type, adapted to exactly this environment, heavy-bodied and happy in mud, and still used to plough paddies a tractor cannot reach. They are working animals, not props. Keep your distance, and do not treat the farmer as a photo opportunity; ask first, and accept no for an answer. Farmers here have been photographed for forty years.

A word about who farms and who lives here. Guangxi is officially the Zhuang Autonomous Region, and the Zhuang — a Tai-speaking people and China's largest ethnic minority, about nineteen million strong — are the reason for the name. Yangshuo county, though, is mostly Han Chinese, and the language you hear in the fields is not Zhuang but a local Southwestern Mandarin, close to the Mandarin you would learn in a classroom and spoken with a Guilin accent. English is a West Street phenomenon; out here, a smile and a phone translator get you further.

And the tension you may already feel: this valley is farmland that happens to be world-famous. Farmers increasingly plant cash crops — pomelos, tangerines, mandarins — because fruit pays better than rice, and many rent rooms to cyclists and rafters. Some of that money is welcome; some of it changes the village. Both things are true. Ride through slowly, keep to the lanes, and if you buy a drink from a farmhouse you have done your bit.

The bamboo rafts you see are the Yulong's signature. They are poled, not motored, down a river punctuated by weirs — low stone dams built roughly every kilometre so animals and people can cross, and so the rafts can shoot the drop in a small wet thrill. The classic ride, from Jinlong Bridge down to Jiuxian, is about six kilometres and ninety minutes and costs around ¥320 per raft for two people; shorter stretches start much cheaper. Prices shift, so verify at the wharf, and never raft when the water is brown and fast — this river floods suddenly after rain.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free — this is farmland and public lanes. Raft rides charge separately: the classic Jinlong Bridge–Jiuxian stretch is around ¥320 per raft for two, shorter hops much less. Verify at the wharf.
stops.openingHours: Open access; best in daylight. Rafts run roughly 08:00 to 17:00 and stop in bad weather or high water.
stops.accessibility: Flat but rough country lanes and field paths; muddy and slippery after rain. Not suitable for wheelchairs, and best on a bicycle.
stops.insiderTip: Ask before photographing anyone working, and never pose farmers or rafters. The buffalo are working animals, so keep clear. The best light on the paddies is early morning and the hour before dusk.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north-west up the valley for about five kilometres to Jiuxian, the old village on the river bank — roughly twenty-five minutes by bike, or about an hour and three-quarters on foot. Our final stop.

stops.name: Jiuxian Village on the Yulong
stops.narration:
You have reached the quiet end of the ride. Jiuxian means "old county town" — the name says the village once held the county administration, and it still keeps a cluster of old houses: grey brick, timber frames, tiled roofs, carved door lintels, some of them Ming and Qing work. Upstream a few kilometres stands the Yulong Bridge, a stone arch about four hundred years old and the reason the river has its name — the water was once called Anle, "peace and joy", and was renamed after the bridge. That is where the classic raft trip begins, and where the prettiest stretch of the river is.

Stand here and put the day together. You started on a street laid out in 590 CE, walked the town, then rode out through the karst to this farming village on a tributary that tourists barely knew existed forty years ago. In between lies the whole bargain of Yangshuo. The karst made the scenery; the river made the route; the backpackers made the reputation; the reputation made the crowds; and the crowds are now the county's living. The villages at the end of this ride are where that bargain is still being negotiated every season, between rice and pomelos and guesthouse rooms.

If the light is going, stay a while. The rafts come down through the weirs in the late afternoon, the buffalo are walked home, and the towers turn blue. This is the Yangshuo the postcards are made from, and it is also somebody's actual farm.

One last thing for another day: the view on your money. The scene printed on the back of the twenty-yuan note is the Li River at Huangbu Shoal, downriver at Xingping, with Yuanbao Mountain behind it — half an hour by road from town, and worth a morning by itself.

For now, get back on the bike before dark. The lanes are unlit, the buffalo have right of way, and the beer fish in town will taste better for the kilometres behind you.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to wander the village lanes. Some old houses charge a small entry; verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Open access. The village is lived in, so keep to the lanes and stay quiet in the evening.
stops.accessibility: Village lanes are uneven stone and packed earth, with some steps and raised thresholds. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the riverbank at dusk: the rafts come down through the weirs in the last light and the towers go blue. Upstream a few kilometres stands the four-hundred-year-old Yulong Bridge, the start of the classic raft trip.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the ride. Turn the bike around and pedal back to town before dark — the lanes are unlit and the buffalo have right of way — and finish with beer fish on West Street. If you have time, Impression Liu Sanjie plays back in town in the evening, and the twenty-yuan-note view waits half an hour downriver at Xingping. You started on a sixth-century street and have ended in a farming village on a tributary tourists barely knew existed forty years ago: that is the whole bargain of Yangshuo, walked and then ridden.
